newsitem.title: JAPAN: NISSAN EYEING DEAL WITH AUTOMAKERS .
newsitem.headline: NISSAN EYEING DEAL WITH AUTOMAKERS .

text.p: Nissan Motor Co Ltd may take a stake in Automakers Ltd , which produces Nissan autos in South Africa, industry sources said on Wednesday.

It is a possibility that Nissan will take a capital stake in Automakers. Nissan doesn't want to fall behind Toyota in controlling its South African unit," said one analyst at a major research company who declined to be named.
Shares in Automakers soared on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange last week on rumours that Nissan and Italy's Fiat SpA were contemplating taking a stake in the carmaker.
On Monday, Automakers said it will delist from the exchange in a move to bring in an unidentified minority shareholder.
A Nissan spokeswoman on Wednesday said she could not confirm or deny such rumours. In Johannesburg, an Automakers spokesman has also declined to confirm a deal was in the works.
Automakers is 50.7 percent owned by Sankorp, 8.7 percent by Mitsui & Co Ltd , and 4.3 percent by Nissan Diesel Co Ltd . Sankorp is an investment company of Sanlam, a South African insurer.

It is the holding company of Nissan South Africa Ltd, which was set up in 1983 to assemble Nissan cars and produced 42,000 Nissan-designed cars in 1995. It also produces about 17,000 Unos for Fiat SpA's a year, and some 2,000 Nissan Diesel Motor Co Ltd-designed trucks annually.
Nissan has no stake in NSA nor Automakers.

Last October, Toyota Motor Corp bought a 27.8 percent stake in Toyota South Africa Ltd (TSA) for 446 million rand to boost its global competitiveness. TSA is 50 percent owned by Wesco, an independent South African holding company.

"We don't know anything about the other company's movement, but if Nissan invests capital in Automakers, we will welcome it very much," said Hiroshi Ariga, a Nissan Diesel senior managing director for export and overseas operations told Reuters.
Nissan Diesel is owned 39.8 percent by Nissan.

"Even if Nissan were to take a stake in the South African firm, it would not be a big burden since it might not cost much money, said another industry analyst who also declined to be named. Like Toyota, they can increase competitiveness in the South African market, which is becoming tougher, and it also gives them access to emerging markets."
